full_judgment:
The word "sentence" as employed in the aforesaid Article, in my opinion, means the final sentence passed by the Court either on the appeal or revision in the High Court Division and also on appeal before the Appellate Division pursuant to a leave petition filed by the aggrieved party. Because the hierarchy of Courts established under the law and Constitution has definite purpose and section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 103 of the Constitution providing for appeal should not be construed as an idle formality or a decoration piece. In other words, the date of conviction and sentence pronounced by the trial Court should not be taken to be the starting point for the disqualification against the convict sitting Member on account of such conviction in a criminal case involving moral turpitude. 

 25. Petitioner was convicted for corruption in Janata Tower Case and was sentenced to 7 years simple imprisonment and then on appeal before High Court Division the sentence was reduced from 7 to 5 years but a fine to the extent of Taka 48,70,800 was imposed by a judgment dated 24-8-2000. A provisional leave petition was filed by the petitioner against the said judgment before the Appellate Division on 27-8-2000 which was subsequently converted into a regular leave petition on 26-10-2000 on receipt of the certified copy of the judgment of the High Court Division. This leave petition was finally heard and dismissed by the Appellate Division on 23-11-2000. The Appellate Division while dismissing the leave petition modified the sentence from 5 years to 3 years and 8 months being the period undergone by the petitioner and the fine as imposed by the High Court Division was maintained. From this order of Appellate Division it is also clear that the forum created for the aggrieved person for relief under Article 103 of the Constitution is real and not just an idle formality. 

 26. The petitioner by invoking Article 103 of the Constitution succeeded in having his sentence reduced substantially and if in case the sentence was reduced below two years the petitioner could very well avoid being disqualified as contemplated under Article 66(2) (d) of the Constitution. The aggrieved person should therefore be allowed to go upto the Appellate Division by filing a leave petition under Article 103 of the Constitution and until that forum is exhausted his conviction and sentence cannot be taken to be final and conclusive for the disqualification to operate. This view finds support from the penultimate paragraph in Form (B) of Schedule III to the Rules of Procedure of Parliament set out and discussed herein below in some detail. Relevant portion of Form (B) is reproduced as under: 

 30. The Speaker after being elected from among the elected Members after a general election as provided under Article 74 of the Constitution becomes the mainstay of the Parliament. The affairs and the general administration of the Parliament are regulated and conducted by the Rules of Procedure made by the Parliament in exercise of its power under Article 75(1) of the Constitution. The Speaker performs his duties and functions through the Parliament Secretariat established under Article 79 of the Constitution. One of such functions of the Speaker is to keep himself posted with the intimation as to the arrest, imprisonment and release of the Members involved in any criminal case or detention made by any executive authority. Rules 172 and 173 of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament are relevant in this connection. When a Member is arrested in a criminal case or is sentenced to imprisonment after conviction by a Court or is detained under an executive order or if he is released on bail pending an appeal or otherwise released, such fact shall be intimated to the Speaker by the concerned Courts including the Supreme Court or the executive authority as the case may be in the appropriate form set out in Schedule III to the Rules. It is also clearly indicated in the penultimate paragraph in Form (B) of Schedule III that the aggrieved Member has a right to seek leave of the Appellate Division under Article 103 of the Constitution for filing an appeal against any judgment and order passed by the High Court, Division against him. If any Member had filed any petition for leave to appeal to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court, the Supreme Court acting through its Registrar should intimate this fact to the Speaker. Similarly, the Supreme Court shall also inform the outcome of the leave petition to the Speaker. The Speaker shall soon thereafter inform the position of the Member concerned to the House, if in session or direct the same to be circulated for information of the Member, if the House is not in session, vide Rule 176. In order to appreciate this position it would be useful to reproduce the said Rules and the Schedule which are as under: 

 37. Mr KS Nabi, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the notification dated 30-8-2000 (Annexure-A) was issued on a misconception of the constitutional provision embodied in clause 2 of Articles 66 when the conviction of the petitioner was not finally decided by the Appellate Division, the apex court of the country, as such, the impugned notification was absolutely without any lawful authority, as such, illegal and was of no legal effect. According to Mr KS Nabi, although the petitioner was found guilty and was convicted under the provisions of Anti- corruption Law and was sentenced to simple imprisonment for a period of seven years by the trial Court but it cannot be said that he was disqualified within the meaning of sub-clause (d) of clause (2) of Article 66 of the Constitution. Because the petitioner's disqualification, as stated therein, is dependent on his conviction involving his moral turpitude and sentenced at least for a period of two years but the petitioner like any other accused has a right of appeal under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the High Court Division and has also a right to file a petition for Leave to Appeal, under Article 103 of the Constitution, before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and thereafter has a further right to file a petition for Leave to Review under Article 105. The learned Advocate submits that till his Leave Petition for Review, which is still pending, is finally decided by the highest Court of the country, no notification declaring his parliamentary seat vacant, can be issued, as such, the impugned notification issued on 30-8-2000, when his provisional petition for Leave to Appeal was pending before the Appellate Division, was absolutely illegal and without any lawful authority, because the question of his conviction was not finally decided till then and since his right to file a leave to appeal before that Appellate Division is a right guaranteed under Article 103, he cannot be said to be a convict within the meaning of sub-clause (d) of clause (2) of Article 66 of the Constitution on 30-8-2000 He submits that the impugned notification being premature and issued on a misconception of the aforesaid provisions of the Constitution and without deciding whether his conviction involved moral turpitude also, as such, was illegal and without any lawful authority. 

 47. Mr KS Nabi wants us to read the words on conviction appearing in sub-clause (d) of clause (2) of Article 66 as 'on final conviction', because, according to him, before disqualification of a member of parliament becomes effective, his appeal and review against the earlier order of conviction must be finally disposed of by the Appellate Division under Article 103 and Article 105 of the Constitution. This argument is fallacious and cannot be accepted. A Court of Law has got no power to add or omit any thing to what is provided in the law itself. The Constitution of the Republic being the Supreme Law of the country, this Court would never embark on such adventure. Rather the learned Judges of the Supreme Court are oath bound to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the laws of Bangladesh. This Court can always explain and expound the Constitutional provisions and other laws of the country but in doing so certainly would never make detour from such laws or even from the spirit of such laws. 

 72. Mr Nabi next submits that although the petitioner like any other convict has got a right of appeal but he will be seriously prejudiced, if he is declared disqualified on his conviction by the trial Court alone, causing serious hardship and injustice on him as a member of Parliament, which cannot be the intent and report of law. From that view of the matter also, he submits, the question of his disqualification can only come up when his appeal is finally disposed of by the Appellate Division under Article 103 and then on Review under Article 105 of the Constitution.
